script.opening: "Hello doctor. I've got this horrible painful rash come up on one side of my forehead, all blistery, and it really burns and stings. I thought maybe it was a bad reaction to a new face cream, or a cold sore gone mad. My eye on that side's a bit red and watery too. Could you give me a cream for it? It's only been a couple of days."

facts.text: Started two days ago on the right side of your forehead going up into the scalp, after a day of burning, tingling pain there. Clusters of small blisters on red skin. It stops at the middle of your forehead. On video: right forehead and scalp, and if asked to look in a mirror — "Oh, there are a couple of blisters on the side and tip of my nose too."
Right eye red, watery, gritty since yesterday. Mild ache. If asked to check: vision slightly blurry in the right eye compared with the left. Light is a bit uncomfortable.
"Burning, stabbing" — 7/10. Paracetamol barely helps. Not sleeping.
Feel a bit run down, no high fever, no headache apart from the rash area, no confusion, no neck stiffness, no vomiting.
Rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate weekly (and folic acid). No allergies. Had chickenpox as a child. Not had the shingles vaccine — "I kept meaning to."
Your daughter is 30 weeks pregnant and was planning to visit at the weekend. You look after your granddaughter, aged 4, on Tuesdays.
67, retired. Lives with husband, who can drive you.
You are worried the methotrexate "caused" it and that you will have to stop it — "my hands were awful before". Say this only if asked what worries you, or if the doctor mentions the methotrexate.

In pain, keen on a cream. When asked to check your nose and eye, report honestly. If told it is shingles near the eye and needs an eye specialist today and antiviral tablets, you are shocked but cooperative. Ask: "Can I still see my daughter at the weekend?" and "Do I stop the methotrexate?"

ice.ideas: "A reaction to my new face cream, or a cold sore gone mad."
ice.concerns: The pain, and (only if asked) the methotrexate and seeing your pregnant daughter.
ice.expectations: "A cream for it." You will go to the eye clinic today if the reason is explained.

cues: "My eye on that side's a bit red and watery too." — say in the opening.
"It's only been a couple of days." — say in the opening.
"I'm on methotrexate — is that a problem?" — say when tablets are discussed.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SHINGLES (herpes zoster): a painful, dermatomal, unilateral, blistering rash not crossing the midline with a prodrome — NOT a cold sore/allergy/cream reaction — and identifies the OPHTHALMIC (V1) distribution

Identifies HERPES ZOSTER OPHTHALMICUS with HUTCHINSON’S SIGN (rash on the side/tip of the nose) and eye involvement (red, gritty, watery eye) as a SIGHT-THREATENING emergency requiring SAME-DAY ophthalmology assessment

Starts oral ANTIVIRALS promptly (within the ~72-hour window; and indicated regardless here given ophthalmic involvement and immunosuppression) at the correct dose, recognising the methotrexate/immunosuppression as a further indication

Manages PAIN adequately and counsels POST-HERPETIC NEURALGIA risk (common, especially older patients), and gives infection-control advice (avoid contact with the immunosuppressed, pregnant women, and non-immune neonates until lesions crust)
Addresses the methotrexate concern appropriately (it did not "cause" shingles but immunosuppression raises risk/severity; do not stop it without advice) and considers the broader picture
Conveys the eye-risk and urgency CLEARLY but calmly so she accepts same-day ophthalmology, without inducing panic; surfaces the "don’t want to make a fuss"/event worry
Validates the pain and fear and explains why this is more than a cream, engaging her in the urgent plan

Safety-nets emphatically: same-day ophthalmology for the eye; any visual change/severe eye pain → emergency eye care; antivirals started; analgesia and PHN safety-net; infection-control advice; and follow-up — sight protected, shingles treated

worked.txt: "This isn’t a cold sore or a cream reaction — it’s shingles: the chickenpox virus reactivating in one nerve, which is why it’s painful, blistery, and in a band on just one side. The good news is you’ve come early, which matters for treatment. But there’s one thing about WHERE yours is that makes me want to act urgently."

"Your rash goes onto the side of your nose, and your eye on that side is red and gritty. That’s an important warning sign — it means the nerve to your EYE is involved, and shingles there can affect your sight if it’s not treated quickly. So this is more than a cream; I need an eye specialist to see you TODAY."

"I’m starting you on antiviral tablets right away — they work best started early like this, and with your eye involved and your arthritis medication lowering your immunity a bit, they’re definitely the right thing. Take them as prescribed; they help the rash and reduce complications."

"Shingles can be very painful, so let’s get on top of that properly — and I’ll be honest that sometimes the nerve pain lingers after the rash heals; if it does, there are specific treatments for it, so tell me. Don’t suffer in silence with the pain."

"You might be wondering if your arthritis tablet caused this — it didn’t cause it, but because it dampens the immune system it can make shingles more likely and a bit more serious, which is another reason we treat promptly. Don’t stop the methotrexate on your own — we’ll take advice on that."

"So: antivirals now, and I’m arranging for the eye team to see you today — if your vision changes or the eye becomes very painful before then, go straight to eye casualty. Keep the rash covered, and avoid anyone who’s pregnant, a newborn, or has a weak immune system until it crusts over. I know you didn’t want a fuss — but protecting your sight is worth it. I’ll follow up how you’re doing."

f.learning: A painful, dermatomal, unilateral, blistering rash that doesn’t cross the midline, with a prodrome of pain/tingling, is shingles (herpes zoster) — not a cold sore or allergy — and oral antivirals should start promptly (ideally within ~72 hours; and regardless here given ophthalmic involvement and immunosuppression). The examinable emergency is HERPES ZOSTER OPHTHALMICUS: rash in the ophthalmic (V1) distribution involving the side/tip of the nose (HUTCHINSON’S SIGN — nasociliary nerve) with a red, gritty eye threatens the eye (keratitis, uveitis, vision loss) and needs SAME-DAY ophthalmology assessment — the eye involvement transforms a "give me a cream" consultation into a sight-saving one. Manage pain and counsel post-herpetic neuralgia (common in older patients), give infection-control advice (avoid contact with the immunosuppressed, pregnant women, non-immune neonates until crusted), and address the methotrexate concern (it didn’t cause it, but immunosuppression raises risk/severity; don’t stop without advice). The hidden agenda is "don’t want to make a fuss"/event worry; convey the eye risk clearly but calmly and act urgently.

knowledge.guideline: UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a (shingles) · SPCs (aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir) · NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain) · College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines (herpes zoster ophthalmicus)
knowledge.summary: A painful, one-sided, blistering rash in a band after a prodrome of pain is shingles. In the ophthalmic division with a rash on the side or tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) and a red eye, it is herpes zoster ophthalmicus: start an oral antiviral today and arrange same-day eye assessment.

points.t: Unilateral, dermatomal, painful vesicular rash that does not cross the midline, often after a day or two of pain or tingling. Cold sores are small, localised and recurrent; contact dermatitis itches rather than burns and is not dermatomal.

Vesicles on the side or tip of the nose involve the nasociliary branch and predict eye involvement (College of Optometrists CMG). With a red, watery or gritty eye, arrange same-day ophthalmology assessment; reduced vision or severe eye pain means emergency eye care.

Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days, valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily for 7 days (SPC/BNF; adjust for renal function). Ophthalmic zoster is always treated; treatment is still considered up to a week after onset if immunosuppressed or new vesicles are forming (NHS England Pharmacy First shingles pathway, 2025). Check BNF interactions with methotrexate.

Treat acute pain adequately. If pain persists after the rash heals, NICE CG173 offers a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (doses per BNF). Older age raises the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia.

Methotrexate did not cause shingles, but immunosuppression raises its risk and severity. Do not tell her to stop it on her own; take advice from her rheumatology team. Avoid adding an NSAID without checking the BNF interaction.

Lesions can transmit chickenpox to non-immune people until crusted. Cover the rash and avoid pregnant women, newborns and immunosuppressed people. After recovery, check Shingrix eligibility against Green Book chapter 28a.

model.text: Hello Mrs Hart, thanks for joining the video call. Tell me about this rash.

It came up two days ago on my forehead, one side, all blistery. It burns and stings. I thought it was a reaction to a new face cream, or a cold sore gone mad. My eye on that side is a bit red and watery too. Could you just give me a cream?
That sounds really painful. I’d like to understand it properly, and I’d like to see it on the camera too, if that’s alright. Then we’ll decide on the right treatment together.
model.why: Sets the agenda and plans a visual assessment

model.text: Of course.
Did you feel anything in that area before the blisters appeared?
A day of tingling and a sort of burning ache, before anything showed.
Could you move the camera close to your face? Show me where the rash goes, including your nose.
model.why: Remote inspection for dermatomal pattern and Hutchinson’s sign

model.text: (angles camera) Here, across the forehead into the hair. And there are a couple of spots on the side of my nose.
Thank you. It stops at the middle of your forehead and doesn’t cross over, and it reaches the side of your nose. Tell me about the eye. Is your vision blurred? Is it painful, or sensitive to light?
model.why: Checks the midline and screens for eye involvement

model.text: It feels gritty and it’s watering. The vision’s maybe a bit blurry, but I thought that was the watering.
You mentioned you take methotrexate. What is that for, and do you take any other medicines? Any kidney problems that you know of?
For my arthritis. That’s the main one. No kidney problems that I know of.
Do you feel unwell in yourself, or feverish? Any rash anywhere else on your body?
model.why: Screens for systemic illness and disseminated zoster

model.text: A bit washed out, but no fever that I’ve noticed. Nothing anywhere else.
You said you were hoping for a cream. What’s been worrying you about it?

Honestly, the pain has frightened me, and the eye. But I didn’t want to make a fuss. We’ve got a family event coming up and I don’t want to be stuck at the hospital. And I did wonder if my arthritis tablets caused it.
Thank you for telling me all of that. You’re not making a fuss. Those are exactly the right things to mention.

This isn’t a cold sore or a reaction to a cream. It’s shingles: the chickenpox virus waking up in one nerve, which is why it’s painful and sits in a band on one side. The spots on the side of your nose matter. They tell me the nerve that supplies your eye is involved, and shingles in the eye can damage sight if it isn’t treated quickly.
model.why: Names shingles and explains Hutchinson’s sign in plain language

model.text: My sight? Goodness.
I know that sounds frightening. The good news is that you’ve come early, and there’s effective treatment. That’s why I want to act today rather than give you a cream.
model.why: Conveys urgency calmly and gives hope

model.text: About the methotrexate: it didn’t cause the shingles, but it lowers your immunity a little, which can make shingles more likely and more severe. Please don’t stop it on your own. I’ll ask your rheumatology team today what they’d like you to do.

So, three things. First, antiviral tablets starting today, which I’ll send to your pharmacy now. Second, I’m arranging for the eye team to see you today. Third, proper pain relief. Can you get to the eye unit this afternoon?
I can get a lift. What about the family event?

It’s a fair question. Let’s see what the eye team says. With treatment most people improve over a couple of weeks. Until the blisters have crusted over, keep the rash covered and stay away from anyone pregnant, newborn babies, or people with weak immunity.
model.why: Infection-control advice, links to her event concern

model.text: Sometimes the nerve pain lingers after the rash heals. If it does, tell me, because there are specific treatments for that kind of pain.
What can I take for the pain now?

Regular paracetamol to start with. Please don’t add ibuprofen from the chemist, because it doesn’t mix well with methotrexate. If the pain isn’t controlled, ring me and I’ll prescribe something stronger that is safe with your other medicine.
model.why: Analgesia with the methotrexate interaction in mind

model.text: If your vision gets worse, the eye becomes very painful, or you can’t bear light before you’re seen, go straight to eye casualty or A&E. Please don’t drive yourself while that eye is affected. Can you tell me the plan back?
Tablets from the chemist today, eye unit this afternoon with a lift, not driving, keep it covered, and don’t stop the methotrexate until you’ve spoken to the rheumatology team.
Perfect. I’ll ring you tomorrow to see how you are and what the eye team said.
Thank you. I’m glad I didn’t just buy a cream.

social.t: Her worry about an upcoming family event may pull her away from same-day care. Acknowledge it and let the eye assessment guide what is realistic.
Ask how she will get there. She should not drive with an affected eye; help her plan a lift or transport.

legal.t: Drivers must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres and meet the DVLA visual acuity standard. Advise her not to drive while vision in the affected eye is blurred or the eye is too painful to open.

professional.t: Changes to a specialist-initiated DMARD during infection should be agreed with the rheumatology team; document the advice given and who gave it.
A camera inspection is enough to recognise Hutchinson’s sign, but eye involvement needs slit-lamp assessment in person. Document why same-day ophthalmology was arranged.

community.t: NHS information on shingles; the community pharmacy for dispensing the antiviral promptly. Note that ophthalmic shingles is outside the community pharmacy shingles pathway.

redFlags: Rash on the side or tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign)
Red, painful or gritty eye, blurred vision, photophobia
psychosocial: Who can take her to hospital; no driving with an affected eye
ice: Idea: "a cold sore gone mad, or a reaction to a face cream"
Concern: the pain, the eye, and whether methotrexate caused it
Expectation: a cream and to carry on

playbook.diagnosis: Herpes zoster in the right ophthalmic division (V1), day 2, with Hutchinson’s sign and a red, watery, gritty eye: herpes zoster ophthalmicus with probable ocular involvement, in an immunosuppressed patient.
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Shingles is the chickenpox virus waking up in one nerve. Yours is in the nerve that also supplies your eye, which is why we treat it with tablets today and ask the eye doctors to check your eye this afternoon."

management.reflectIce: "You didn’t want to make a fuss, and you were worried about your eye and your arthritis tablets. Mentioning the eye was exactly the right thing to do."
management.psychosocial: Link the plan to her family event; help her plan transport; no driving with the affected eye.
sharedPlan: Oral antiviral today: aciclovir 800 mg five times daily, or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily, or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily, each for 7 days (SPC/BNF; check renal function and methotrexate interaction)
Analgesia; PHN counselling (NICE CG173 options if it develops); same-day rheumatology advice on methotrexate; cover the rash and avoid vulnerable contacts until crusted
safetyNet: Worsening vision, severe eye pain or photophobia: eye casualty or A&E immediately
Telephone follow-up next day; review if new areas of rash or feeling systemically unwell; check Shingrix eligibility after recovery

pitfalls.intro: This station hides a sight-threatening emergency inside a request for a cream. Candidates fail by accepting her label, missing the nose and the eye, or mishandling the methotrexate. These are the recurring patterns.

items.fail: Accepting "cold sore" or "cream reaction" and prescribing a topical.
items.why: "Did not reach an appropriate diagnosis." A dermatomal, painful, vesicular rash with a prodrome is shingles.
items.fix: Ask about the prodrome and look at the pattern: one side, a band, not crossing the midline.

items.fail: Starting an antiviral but not arranging same-day eye assessment.
items.why: Hutchinson’s sign with a red, gritty eye signals ocular involvement; missing same-day ophthalmology is a safety failure.
items.fix: Ask her to show the side of her nose, ask about the eye, and arrange ophthalmology today.

items.fail: Telling her to stop methotrexate, or ignoring it entirely.
items.why: Both are unsafe: one risks a flare without specialist advice, the other misses a reason for treatment and an interaction check.
items.fix: "It didn’t cause this, but it lowers immunity. Don’t stop it; I’ll speak to rheumatology today."

items.fail: Brushing past "I don’t want to make a fuss" and the family event.
items.why: "Did not explore the patient’s concerns." These are the reasons she may not go to the eye unit.
items.fix: Name them and link the plan: "Let’s get your eye checked today so we know what’s realistic for the event."

items.why: Frightening wording without context is marked as poor explanation and may paralyse rather than motivate.
items.fix: Explain calmly why the nose matters, then give the hopeful part: early treatment works.

items.fail: No mention of post-herpetic neuralgia or infection control.
items.why: An incomplete plan loses Tasks marks even with the right antiviral.
items.fix: One sentence each: lingering nerve pain can be treated; cover the rash and avoid pregnant women, newborns and immunosuppressed people until crusted.

items.fail: Closing without saying what to do if vision worsens before she is seen.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: "Worse vision, severe pain or light sensitivity: eye casualty straight away. Don’t drive. I’ll ring you tomorrow."

Prodrome, dermatomal pattern, midline, nose (Hutchinson’s sign), vision, pain, photophobia, methotrexate, renal function.
Pain and eye fear, "don’t want a fuss", the family event, did the methotrexate cause it?
Shingles, not a cold sore. The eye is involved. Antiviral today, same-day ophthalmology, analgesia, methotrexate advice, infection control, PHN.

wordPics.fail: Accepts the cold sore or allergy label and gives a cream; misses Hutchinson’s sign and the eye; no antiviral, or antiviral but no same-day eye assessment; tells her to stop methotrexate; no safety-net for visual change.
wordPics.pass: Recognises shingles in the ophthalmic division; starts an oral antiviral at a correct dose; arranges same-day ophthalmology; gives analgesia and infection-control advice; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains Hutchinson’s sign in plain words without frightening her; addresses the methotrexate worry accurately and seeks rheumatology advice; responds to the family-event worry; counsels PHN; advises about driving; checks understanding and arranges personal follow-up.

avoid.dont: "It’s probably a cold sore. Here’s some aciclovir cream."
avoid.instead: "This is shingles, and because it reaches the side of your nose it may affect your eye, so you need tablets and an eye check today."
avoid.why: Topical treatment and a missed ophthalmic zoster is a sight-threatening error.

avoid.instead: "Please carry on for now. I’ll ask your rheumatology team today what they’d like you to do."
avoid.why: Stopping a DMARD without specialist advice risks a flare and is outside safe practice.

avoid.dont: "You could lose your sight in that eye."
avoid.instead: "Shingles near the eye can affect sight if it isn’t treated quickly, which is why we’re acting today."
avoid.why: The same message, framed calmly, gets her to the eye unit without panic.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: UKHSA Green Book chapter 28a (shingles) · SPCs (aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir) · NICE CG173 (neuropathic pain) · College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines (herpes zoster ophthalmicus)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A painful, one-sided, blistering rash in a band after a prodrome of pain is shingles. In the ophthalmic division with a rash on the side or tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) and a red eye, it is herpes zoster ophthalmicus: start an oral antiviral today and arrange same-day eye assessment.

points.t: Unilateral, dermatomal, painful vesicular rash that does not cross the midline, often after a day or two of pain or tingling. Cold sores are small, localised and recurrent; contact dermatitis itches rather than burns and is not dermatomal.

Vesicles on the side or tip of the nose involve the nasociliary branch and predict eye involvement (College of Optometrists CMG). With a red, watery or gritty eye, arrange same-day ophthalmology assessment; reduced vision or severe eye pain means emergency eye care.

Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days, valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days, or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily for 7 days (SPC/BNF; adjust for renal function). Ophthalmic zoster is always treated; treatment is still considered up to a week after onset if immunosuppressed or new vesicles are forming (NHS England Pharmacy First shingles pathway, 2025). Check BNF interactions with methotrexate.

Treat acute pain adequately. If pain persists after the rash heals, NICE CG173 offers a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin (doses per BNF). Older age raises the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia.

Methotrexate did not cause shingles, but immunosuppression raises its risk and severity. Do not tell her to stop it on her own; take advice from her rheumatology team. Avoid adding an NSAID without checking the BNF interaction.

Lesions can transmit chickenpox to non-immune people until crusted. Cover the rash and avoid pregnant women, newborns and immunosuppressed people. After recovery, check Shingrix eligibility against Green Book chapter 28a.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the rash and ask for a cream before redirecting.
Family event and travel worries; who can take her to the eye unit; reluctance to make a fuss.
Picked up the red, watery eye and the "arthritis tablets" comment and explored both.
Idea (cold sore or cream reaction), concerns (pain, eye, methotrexate, the event), expectation (a cream).
Camera inspection of the dermatomal pattern, midline and nose; visual symptoms, photophobia and pain; renal function and interactions.
Shingles versus cold sore versus contact dermatitis; ocular involvement (keratitis, uveitis).
Identified Hutchinson’s sign and eye symptoms as sight-threatening herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
Named ophthalmic shingles in plain language and explained why it is urgent.
Oral antiviral today at the correct dose, same-day ophthalmology, analgesia, infection-control advice.
Methotrexate: not the cause, do not stop without advice, same-day rheumatology input; NSAID interaction checked.
Emergency eye care for visual change or severe pain, no driving, PHN counselling, next-day telephone follow-up.

social.t: Her worry about an upcoming family event may pull her away from same-day care. Acknowledge it and let the eye assessment guide what is realistic.
Ask how she will get there. She should not drive with an affected eye; help her plan a lift or transport.

legal.t: Drivers must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres and meet the DVLA visual acuity standard. Advise her not to drive while vision in the affected eye is blurred or the eye is too painful to open.

professional.t: Changes to a specialist-initiated DMARD during infection should be agreed with the rheumatology team; document the advice given and who gave it.
A camera inspection is enough to recognise Hutchinson’s sign, but eye involvement needs slit-lamp assessment in person. Document why same-day ophthalmology was arranged.

community.t: NHS information on shingles; the community pharmacy for dispensing the antiviral promptly. Note that ophthalmic shingles is outside the community pharmacy shingles pathway.

redFlags: Rash on the side or tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign)
Red, painful or gritty eye, blurred vision, photophobia
psychosocial: Who can take her to hospital; no driving with an affected eye
ice: Idea: "a cold sore gone mad, or a reaction to a face cream"
Concern: the pain, the eye, and whether methotrexate caused it
Expectation: a cream and to carry on

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Herpes zoster in the right ophthalmic division (V1), day 2, with Hutchinson’s sign and a red, watery, gritty eye: herpes zoster ophthalmicus with probable ocular involvement, in an immunosuppressed patient.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "Shingles is the chickenpox virus waking up in one nerve. Yours is in the nerve that also supplies your eye, which is why we treat it with tablets today and ask the eye doctors to check your eye this afternoon."

management.reflectIce: "You didn’t want to make a fuss, and you were worried about your eye and your arthritis tablets. Mentioning the eye was exactly the right thing to do."
management.psychosocial: Link the plan to her family event; help her plan transport; no driving with the affected eye.
sharedPlan: Oral antiviral today: aciclovir 800 mg five times daily, or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily, or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily, each for 7 days (SPC/BNF; check renal function and methotrexate interaction)
Analgesia; PHN counselling (NICE CG173 options if it develops); same-day rheumatology advice on methotrexate; cover the rash and avoid vulnerable contacts until crusted
safetyNet: Worsening vision, severe eye pain or photophobia: eye casualty or A&E immediately
Telephone follow-up next day; review if new areas of rash or feeling systemically unwell; check Shingrix eligibility after recovery

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hides a sight-threatening emergency inside a request for a cream. Candidates fail by accepting her label, missing the nose and the eye, or mishandling the methotrexate. These are the recurring patterns.

items.fail: Accepting "cold sore" or "cream reaction" and prescribing a topical.
items.why: "Did not reach an appropriate diagnosis." A dermatomal, painful, vesicular rash with a prodrome is shingles.
items.fix: Ask about the prodrome and look at the pattern: one side, a band, not crossing the midline.

items.fail: Starting an antiviral but not arranging same-day eye assessment.
items.why: Hutchinson’s sign with a red, gritty eye signals ocular involvement; missing same-day ophthalmology is a safety failure.
items.fix: Ask her to show the side of her nose, ask about the eye, and arrange ophthalmology today.

items.fail: Telling her to stop methotrexate, or ignoring it entirely.
items.why: Both are unsafe: one risks a flare without specialist advice, the other misses a reason for treatment and an interaction check.
items.fix: "It didn’t cause this, but it lowers immunity. Don’t stop it; I’ll speak to rheumatology today."

items.fail: Brushing past "I don’t want to make a fuss" and the family event.
items.why: "Did not explore the patient’s concerns." These are the reasons she may not go to the eye unit.
items.fix: Name them and link the plan: "Let’s get your eye checked today so we know what’s realistic for the event."

items.why: Frightening wording without context is marked as poor explanation and may paralyse rather than motivate.
items.fix: Explain calmly why the nose matters, then give the hopeful part: early treatment works.

items.fail: No mention of post-herpetic neuralgia or infection control.
items.why: An incomplete plan loses Tasks marks even with the right antiviral.
items.fix: One sentence each: lingering nerve pain can be treated; cover the rash and avoid pregnant women, newborns and immunosuppressed people until crusted.

items.fail: Closing without saying what to do if vision worsens before she is seen.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: "Worse vision, severe pain or light sensitivity: eye casualty straight away. Don’t drive. I’ll ring you tomorrow."
